title: How to Calculate Foreign Tax Credit for RSUs: H-1B Worker Step-by-Step Guide 2026
description: Master Foreign Tax Credit calculations for RSU income. Complete guide with examples, IRS Form 1116 instructions, and strategies to maximize your FTC and reduce tax liability.
content:
## Key Takeaways

- Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) prevents **double taxation** on the same RSU income
- Most H-1B workers leave **$3,000-$8,000** on the table by not claiming FTC properly
- Form 1116 is required for each income category (passive, general, etc.)
- FTC has a **limitation formula** - you can't always claim 100% of foreign tax paid
- Use our [free calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator) to maximize your FTC automatically

## What Is Foreign Tax Credit and Why Does It Matter for RSUs?

Foreign Tax Credit is a **dollar-for-dollar reduction** in your US tax liability for income taxes paid to foreign countries.

**Without FTC:** You pay tax twice on the same income
**With FTC:** You pay the *higher* of the two countries' tax rates (not both)

### Real Example: Why FTC Matters

**Scenario:** You worked 3 years at Amazon Seattle (H-1B), then returned to Toronto. Your 4th-year RSUs ($80,000) vest after you're a Canadian tax resident.

**Without claiming FTC:**
- US withholding: $17,600 (22% federal)
- Canada tax: $28,000 (35% marginal rate)
- **Total tax paid: $45,600** (57% effective rate)

**With FTC:**
- US withholding: $17,600
- Canada tax: $28,000
- Canada FTC: -$17,600
- **Net Canada tax: $10,400**
- **Total tax paid: $28,000** (35% effective rate)
- **Savings: $17,600** (the US tax you claimed as credit)

## Understanding the FTC Limitation Formula

You **cannot** always claim 100% of foreign tax paid. The IRS limits FTC to prevent you from using foreign taxes to offset US domestic income.

### The FTC Limitation Formula

```
FTC Limit = US Tax × (Foreign Source Income / Worldwide Income)
```

**What this means:**
- If 50% of your income is foreign-sourced → You can claim up to 50% of your US tax as FTC
- If foreign tax paid exceeds this limit → Carry it forward up to 10 years

### Example: How the Limitation Works

**Your income:**
- US salary (W-2): $100,000
- Canadian RSU income: $60,000 (allocated per tax treaty)
- **Total worldwide income: $160,000**

**US tax calculation:**
- Tax on $160,000: $32,000 (20% effective rate)

**FTC limitation:**
```
FTC Limit = $32,000 × ($60,000 / $160,000) = $12,000
```

**Foreign tax paid:**
- Canada tax on $60,000: $21,000

**What you can claim:**
- FTC allowed: $12,000 (limited by formula)
- Excess: $9,000 (carry forward to next year)
- **US tax after FTC: $20,000**

**Pro Tip:** Most tax software gets this wrong. Use Form 1116 manually or our [calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator) to verify.

## IRS Form 1116: Line-by-Line Instructions

### When You Must File Form 1116

**Required if:**
- Foreign tax paid >$300 single / $600 married
- Income is from multiple foreign countries
- Income includes capital gains or dividends

**Not required if:**
- Foreign tax paid <$300/$600 AND
- All income is "qualified passive income" (dividends, interest)

**For RSUs:** You **must** file Form 1116 because employment income is "general category," not passive.

### Form 1116 Part I: Taxable Income from Sources Outside the US

**Line 1a:** Enter gross foreign source income
- For RSUs: Enter the Canada-allocated portion only (not total RSU)
- **Example:** $60,000 (based on work period attribution)

**Line 1b:** Deductions definitely allocable to foreign income
- Stock plan fees: $150
- Tax prep fees (prorated): $300
- **Total: $450**

**Line 2:** Deductions not definitely allocable
- Standard deduction: $14,600 × ($60,000 / $160,000) = $5,475

**Line 3a:** Total deductions ($450 + $5,475 = $5,925)

**Line 3e:** Net foreign source taxable income
- $60,000 - $5,925 = **$54,075**

### Form 1116 Part II: Foreign Taxes Paid or Accrued

**Choose one method:**
1. **Cash method:** Taxes actually paid during the year
2. **Accrual method:** Taxes accrued (owed) during the year

**For most H-1B workers:** Use cash method (when you actually paid Canadian tax)

**Line 8:** Enter foreign tax paid
- Canada tax on $60,000 RSU: $21,000 CAD
- Convert to USD: $21,000 ÷ 1.36 FX rate = **$15,441 USD**

**Line 9:** Carryback/carryover from prior years
- If you had excess FTC last year, enter it here
- **Example:** $2,000 carryover from 2025

**Line 10:** Total foreign taxes ($15,441 + $2,000 = $17,441)

### Form 1116 Part III: Figuring the Credit

**Line 14:** Enter taxable income from Form 1040
- **Example:** $160,000

**Line 15:** Adjustments (usually $0 for W-2 workers)

**Line 16:** Enter tax from Form 1040 (before credits)
- **Example:** $32,000

**Line 17:** FTC limitation calculation
```
$32,000 × ($54,075 / $160,000) = $10,815
```

**Line 18:** Enter smaller of:
- Line 10 (foreign tax paid): $17,441
- Line 17 (FTC limit): $10,815
- **Result: $10,815** (this is your allowed FTC)

**Line 19:** Carryback/carryover (if applicable)

**Line 20:** Total Foreign Tax Credit
- Transfer to Form 1040, Schedule 3, Line 48
- **$10,815**

**Excess FTC:**
- Foreign tax paid: $17,441
- FTC allowed: $10,815
- **Excess: $6,626** (carry forward up to 10 years)

## Common FTC Calculation Mistakes

### Mistake 1: Using Wrong Exchange Rate

The IRS requires you to use the exchange rate **on the date you paid the tax**, not the annual average.

**Example:**
- You paid Canada tax on April 30, 2026
- USD/CAD rate on April 30: 1.38
- Annual average rate: 1.36
- **Correct:** Use 1.38 (date of payment)

**Where to find daily rates:** [IRS Yearly Average Currency Exchange Rates](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/yearly-average-currency-exchange-rates)

### Mistake 2: Not Separating Income Categories

Form 1116 requires **separate forms** for each income type:
- General category income (RSUs, salary)
- Passive category income (dividends, interest)
- Section 951A income (GILTI)

**Example:**
- Canadian RSU income: $60,000 → Form 1116 (general)
- Canadian dividend income: $5,000 → Form 1116 (passive)
- **You must file 2 separate Form 1116s**

### Mistake 3: Claiming Provincial Tax for US Purposes

The US only allows FTC for **foreign national taxes**, not subnational (provincial, state).

**Incorrect:**
- Canada federal tax: $12,000
- Ontario provincial tax: $8,000
- Claim FTC for: $20,000 ❌

**Correct:**
- Claim FTC only for Canada federal: $12,000 ✓
- Provincial tax is **not creditable** in the US

**But:** Canada allows FTC for US *state* tax (better than US treatment!)

### Mistake 4: Not Carrying Forward Excess FTC

If your FTC exceeds the limitation, you can carry it:
- **Back 1 year**
- **Forward 10 years**

**Example:**
- 2026 FTC limit: $10,000
- Foreign tax paid: $17,000
- Excess: $7,000

**Don't lose it!** File Form 1116 in 2027 and claim the $7,000 carryover.

**How to track:**
- Keep a spreadsheet: [Year | Excess FTC | Expiry Date]
- 2026 excess expires in 2036

## Special RSU Situations

### Situation 1: Multi-Country RSU Allocation

You worked in 3 countries during the vesting period:
- US (H-1B): 2 years
- Canada (work permit): 1 year
- India (remote): 1 year

**Tax treatment:**
- US portion: 50% → US tax only
- Canada portion: 25% → Canada tax, claim FTC in US
- India portion: 25% → India tax, claim FTC in US

**You need:**
- 2 separate Form 1116s (one for Canada, one for India)
- Proof of Indian tax paid (TDS certificate)
- Work location tracker (daily log)

### Situation 2: Stock Price Changed Between Vesting and Tax Payment

RSUs vested at $100/share, but stock dropped to $80 by the time you paid Canadian tax.

**Question:** Do you use $100 or $80 for FTC calculation?

**Answer:** Use the **vesting day value** ($100) for US purposes, even if Canada taxed a different amount.

**Why:** The IRS doesn't care about fair market value changes post-vesting. FTC is based on the same income source.

### Situation 3: You Paid AMT (Alternative Minimum Tax)

If you're subject to AMT, your FTC is calculated differently:

**Regular tax FTC:**
- Limited by regular tax liability

**AMT FTC:**
- Limited by AMT liability
- Calculated on Form 6251
- You can use the **higher** of the two

**Pro Tip:** If you paid AMT, file Form 1116 *and* Form 6251 to maximize FTC.

## How to Claim FTC in Canada (For Canadian Residents)

If you're a Canadian tax resident with US-sourced RSU income:

### Step 1: Report Foreign Income on T1

**Line 10400:** Enter employment income (including US RSUs)
- Convert USD to CAD using [Bank of Canada annual average rate](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/exchange/annual-average-exchange-rates/)
- **Example:** $60,000 USD × 1.36 = $81,600 CAD

### Step 2: Calculate Canadian Tax

**Schedule 1:** Federal tax
- $81,600 at 26% marginal = $21,216 federal

**Provincial (Ontario):**
- $81,600 at 11.16% = $9,107 provincial

**Total Canada tax:** $30,323 CAD

### Step 3: Claim Foreign Tax Credit (Form T2209)

**Part A: Foreign non-business income tax**

**Line 40500:** Net foreign non-business income
- $81,600 CAD

**Line 40425:** Foreign non-business income tax paid
- US tax paid: $17,600 USD × 1.36 = $23,936 CAD

**Line 40600:** FTC calculation
```
Lesser of:
1. Foreign tax paid: $23,936
2. Canada tax × (Foreign income / Total income)
   = $30,323 × ($81,600 / $120,000) = $20,619

FTC = $20,619
```

**Net Canada tax due:**
- Total tax: $30,323
- Less FTC: $20,619
- **Payable: $9,704 CAD**

**Excess FTC:**
- Foreign tax paid: $23,936
- FTC allowed: $20,619
- **Excess: $3,317** (this is lost in Canada - no carryforward!)

### Canada vs US FTC Rules: Key Differences

| Feature | US (Form 1116) | Canada (Form T2209) |
|---------|----------------|---------------------|
| Carryback | 1 year | ❌ None |
| Carryforward | 10 years | ❌ None |
| Provincial/state tax | ❌ Not creditable | ✅ Creditable |
| Separate categories | ✅ Required | ❌ Not required |
| Inflation adjustment | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |

**Key takeaway:** US FTC rules are more generous (10-year carryforward) but Canada allows state tax credits.

## Strategic FTC Optimization Techniques

### Strategy 1: Timing Tax Payments

If you can control *when* you pay Canadian tax, optimize for FTC.

**Example:**
- 2026 income: $200,000
- 2027 income (projected): $100,000 (taking sabbatical)

**Option A: Pay Canada tax in April 2027**
- High 2026 US tax → High FTC limit → Claim full FTC

**Option B: Pay Canada tax in January 2028**
- Low 2027 US tax → Low FTC limit → Excess FTC wasted

**Best:** Pay in April 2027 (claim on 2026 return with accrual method)

### Strategy 2: Bunch Foreign Income

If you have control over RSU vesting timing, bunch it to maximize FTC.

**Example:**
- Option A: Vest $100K/year for 4 years
- Option B: Accelerate vesting - $400K in Year 1

**Option A:**
- FTC limit each year: $10K
- Total FTC over 4 years: $40K
- Excess FTC: $20K (some lost to 10-year expiry)

**Option B:**
- FTC limit in Year 1: $80K
- Total FTC: $80K (all claimed)
- **Savings: $20K** (no FTC wasted)

### Strategy 3: Convert Passive Income to General

Passive income (dividends, interest) has a *separate* FTC limitation. General income (RSUs, salary) has its own.

**Problem:** You have excess passive FTC that can't offset general income.

**Solution:**
- Invest in PFIC (Passive Foreign Investment Company) that distributes "excess distribution" → treated as ordinary income (general category)
- Converts passive to general → Use excess FTC

**Warning:** PFICs have complex reporting (Form 8621). Only for advanced taxpayers.

## Real Example: Meta H-1B Worker's FTC Calculation

**Profile:**
- Sarah, H-1B worker at Meta Menlo Park (2022-2025)
- Returned to Toronto Jan 2026
- 4-year RSU grant: $320,000 ($80K/year)
- Year 4 vesting: $80,000 (75% US, 25% Canada per treaty)

**Step 1: Allocate Income**
- US portion: $60,000 (75%)
- Canada portion: $20,000 (25%)

**Step 2: Calculate US Tax**
- US income: $60,000
- US tax: $12,000 (20% effective)
- US withholding: $17,600 (on full $80K)
- **US refund: $5,600** (overpaid)

**Step 3: Calculate Canada Tax**
- Canada income: $80,000 CAD
- Canada tax: $28,000 (35% marginal)

**Step 4: Claim FTC in Canada**
- Foreign tax paid: $12,000 USD = $16,320 CAD
- FTC limit: $28,000 × ($80K / $80K) = $28,000
- **FTC allowed: $16,320** (full amount)

**Step 5: Net Result**
- US tax: $12,000 (refunded: $5,600 overpayment)
- Canada tax: $28,000 - $16,320 FTC = $11,680
- **Total tax: $23,680** (29.6% effective rate)

**Without FTC:**
- US tax: $12,000
- Canada tax: $28,000
- **Total: $40,000** (50% rate)
- **FTC savings: $16,320**

## When to Hire a CPA vs DIY

**DIY with our calculator if:**
- Single employer W-2 + RSU income
- Total income <$300K
- Working in only 1-2 countries
- No AMT complications

**Hire a CPA if:**
- Income >$500K (complex FTC limitation scenarios)
- Multiple foreign countries (need separate Form 1116 for each)
- Subject to AMT (requires Form 6251 FTC calculation)
- Self-employment income + RSUs (SE tax complications)
- PFIC investments (Form 8621 + FTC interaction)

**Average CPA cost:** $1,500-$3,500 for dual-country return with FTC

## Action Checklist

**Before filing:**
- [ ] Gather all foreign tax payment receipts (Canada, India, etc.)
- [ ] Find official exchange rates from [IRS](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/yearly-average-currency-exchange-rates) or [Bank of Canada](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/exchange/)
- [ ] Separate income by category (general vs passive)
- [ ] Check for FTC carryovers from prior years

**When filing Form 1116:**
- [ ] File separate forms for each income category
- [ ] Use correct exchange rate (date of payment, not annual average)
- [ ] Calculate FTC limitation properly (most software gets this wrong)
- [ ] Track excess FTC for carryforward (expires in 10 years)

**After filing:**
- [ ] Save Form 1116 and supporting docs for 7 years
- [ ] Create spreadsheet tracking FTC carryovers by year
- [ ] Set calendar reminder to claim carryover next year
